prompt.text: An ordered collection of scores you will keep appending to

why: Lists are ordered and mutable, so appending and reordering later is exactly what they are for.

prompt.text: Pairs of country → capital, looked up by country

why: A dict maps keys to values with O(1) lookup by key; a list would force a linear search.

prompt.text: Unique tags on a post, where duplicates must be impossible

why: A set stores each value once and rejects duplicates automatically.

prompt.text: A fixed (x, y) coordinate that must never change

why: Tuples are immutable: once built, the pair cannot be edited by accident.

prompt.text: Shopping-cart items in the order they were added, duplicates fine

why: Order and duplicates both matter, which rules out a set; a list keeps both.

prompt.text: Word → how many times it appears in a text

why: Counting by key is a mapping job: dict[word] = count.

prompt.text: The seven days of the week, in order, never modified

why: A fixed ordered sequence that never changes is the classic tuple.

prompt.text: Every distinct visitor ID seen today

why: Distinct means no duplicates; sets enforce that and test membership fast.

prompt.text: Lines of a file, in order, which you will edit in place

why: Editing by position needs a mutable ordered sequence: a list.

prompt.text: An RGB colour as three numbers that belong together

why: A small fixed-size record whose positions have meaning is a tuple, not a list.

prompt.text: Student name → grade

why: Look up by name, store the grade: a mapping, so a dict.

prompt.text: The letters used in a word, each counted once

why: set(word) collapses repeats and keeps each character once.

prompt.text: A to-do list the user reorders by dragging

why: Reordering means mutating positions, which only a list allows.

prompt.text: Return two values from a function at once

why: return a, b builds a tuple; callers unpack it as x, y = f().

prompt.text: Needs fast membership checks (is x in here?) over millions of IDs

why: Set membership is O(1) on average via hashing; a list scans every element.

prompt.text: Must be usable as a dictionary key

why: Dict keys must be hashable; tuples of hashable items qualify, lists never do.

prompt.text: A mapping where each key points at a list of values

why: Values can be anything, including lists: dict[key] = [...].

prompt.text: You must sort it in place later

why: Only lists have .sort(); tuples are immutable and sets have no order.

prompt.text: Preserve insertion order AND allow duplicates

why: Sets drop duplicates and dicts need keys; a list keeps every item in order.

prompt.text: Preserve the insertion order of key/value pairs

why: Since Python 3.7 dicts remember insertion order, so iteration is predictable.

prompt.text: Remove duplicates from a sequence quickly when order does not matter

why: set(seq) deduplicates in one pass; use dict.fromkeys(seq) if order must survive.

prompt.text: Index by position AND guarantee immutability

why: Tuples support t[i] and slicing but cannot be changed afterwards.

prompt.text: A memory-light record of a date: (year, month, day)

why: Tuples are smaller than lists and signal a fixed structure to readers.

prompt.text: Configuration settings looked up by name

why: Named lookup is a mapping; settings[name] reads clearly.

prompt.text: Union and intersection of two groups of users

why: Set algebra (|, &, -) is built in and fast; lists have no such operators.

prompt.text: Items accessed by integer position while the length changes often

why: Growing and shrinking by position is list territory.

prompt.text: Keys are strings, values can be anything

why: Heterogeneous values under string keys is exactly a dict.

prompt.text: A group of values you need to hash to cache a function result

why: functools.lru_cache needs hashable arguments; convert a list to a tuple first.

prompt.text: Append AND pop from both ends in O(1)

why: collections.deque is a double-ended queue; list.pop(0) is O(n).

prompt.text: An immutable set you can place inside another set

why: Set elements must be hashable; a frozenset is a hashable, immutable set.

prompt.text: A sliding window over the last 5 sensor readings

why: deque(maxlen=5) drops the oldest reading automatically when a new one arrives.

prompt.text: A bundle of permissions that must work as a dict key

why: A frozenset of permission names is hashable, so it can key a dict or sit in a set.

prompt.text: The frontier of a breadth-first search

why: BFS pops from the front and appends to the back; deque does both in O(1).

prompt.text: Tags on a post that are added and removed freely

why: A regular set is mutable: add() and discard() as tags change.

prompt.text: Constant-time membership for a collection that must never change after creation

why: frozenset gives hashed membership plus immutability.

prompt.text: Browser history where any page can be inspected by index

why: Random access by index is O(1) on a list but O(n) in the middle of a deque.

prompt.text: A task queue: producers append, consumers take from the front

why: popleft() on a deque is O(1); list.pop(0) shifts every remaining element.

prompt.text: A lookup table from (row, col) pairs to values

why: The key is a tuple (row, col) and the structure is a dict keyed by it.

prompt.text: A record returned from a database row, read-only

why: Rows are fixed-width, immutable records: tuples (or namedtuples).

prompt.text: Deduplicated IDs built once and shared read-only across threads

why: Immutability makes sharing safe: nobody can mutate it underneath another reader.

prompt.text: A ring buffer with a fixed capacity that drops the oldest item

why: deque(maxlen=n) is a ring buffer out of the box.

prompt.text: Variable-length ordered data you slice often

why: Slicing and in-place edits of a growing sequence point to a list.

prompt.text: Counts per key with a default of 0

why: dict.get(key, 0) or a defaultdict(int) handles missing keys cleanly.

prompt.text: A collection of friend groups, where each group is itself a set

why: Inner sets must be hashable to live inside an outer set, so they become frozensets.

prompt.text: Repeatedly pop from the front of a million-item collection

why: Front pops are O(1) on a deque and O(n) on a list: a million-fold difference at scale.

prompt.text: Version numbers compared position by position: (3, 11, 2)

why: Tuples compare lexicographically and are immutable, perfect for versions.

prompt.text: Unique elements where you also remove items by value fast

why: set.discard(x) is O(1); list.remove(x) scans the list.

prompt.text: An ordered mapping iterated with .items() in insertion order

why: dicts iterate in insertion order and expose .items() for key/value pairs.

prompt.text: A fixed-size history of the last N shell commands

why: deque(maxlen=N) keeps exactly the last N commands with no manual trimming.

prompt.text: An immutable, hashable collection with duplicates removed

why: Deduplicated plus immutable plus hashable is the definition of a frozenset.

prompt.text: An append-heavy log you occasionally index

why: Appends are amortised O(1) on a list and indexing is O(1); a deque indexes slowly in the middle.

prompt.text: Unique visitors per day where you also need the union across days

why: Sets dedupe and support | for the union of several days.

prompt.text: Add an element to the END of a growing list in O(1) amortised

why: append writes at the end without shifting anything.

prompt.text: Add an element to the FRONT of a deque in O(1)

why: appendleft is the deque's O(1) front insert; a list has no cheap equivalent.

prompt.text: Add a unique element, ignoring it if already present

why: set.add is idempotent: adding an existing value changes nothing.

prompt.text: Read a key but fall back to a default when it is missing

why: dict.get(key, default) avoids KeyError and the if-in dance.

prompt.text: A membership test on a tiny collection of 3 unhashable items

why: With three items a linear scan is trivial, and unhashable items cannot go in a set anyway.

prompt.text: A membership test against 10 million user IDs

why: Hashing makes membership O(1) on average; a list would scan up to 10 million items.

prompt.text: Insert at the front of a list (every element shifts right)

why: insert(0, x) is O(n) because all existing elements move one slot.

prompt.text: Push a task to the back of a queue kept in a plain list

why: The back of a list is where append is cheap.

prompt.text: Keep most-recent-first order by inserting at the front of a deque

why: appendleft puts the newest item first in O(1).

prompt.text: Check whether a list (unhashable) is one of a few stored lists

why: Lists cannot be set members, so a short linear scan is the right tool.

prompt.text: Increment counts[word] safely when the key may not exist yet

why: counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1 handles first sightings.

prompt.text: Dedupe a stream one item at a time

why: Add each item to a set as it arrives; repeats are absorbed.

prompt.text: Check whether a username is already taken, O(1) average

why: Usernames are hashable strings; a set answers membership in constant time.

prompt.text: Append a reading to the end of a plain list

why: Appending to the end is the cheap list operation.

prompt.text: Front insertion when the collection is already a deque

why: deque exists for exactly this: cheap inserts at both ends.

prompt.text: Prepend to a list of 10 items, readability over speed

why: For tiny lists the O(n) shift is negligible and insert(0, x) reads clearly.

prompt.text: Read the theme setting with a fallback of light

why: settings.get(key, default) returns the fallback instead of raising.

prompt.text: Membership in an ordered sequence where order matters and items repeat

why: A list preserves order and duplicates; membership is a scan, which is fine when the list is small.

prompt.text: Add a value to a hash set

why: set.add is the hash-set insert.

prompt.text: Which operation is O(n) because every element shifts right?

why: insert at index 0 moves all n elements; append does not.

prompt.text: Which operation makes a sliding window's front insertion O(1)?

why: deque.appendleft is constant time; list.insert(0) is linear.

prompt.text: Test membership where the items are unhashable dicts

why: dicts cannot be hashed, so a set is impossible; scan the list.

prompt.text: Test membership in O(1) average over a large collection of strings

why: Strings hash well; a set gives constant-time membership.

prompt.text: Push onto a stack implemented with a list

why: A list stack pushes with append and pops with pop(), both at the end.

prompt.text: Fetch an optional config value or None without a KeyError

why: dict.get(key) returns None when the key is missing.

prompt.text: Which membership test is the wrong choice for a million hashable IDs?

why: A list scans linearly; for a million hashable IDs a set is the right tool, which is why this card is the trap.
